basic_information.official_title: AN ACT CREATING THE BANGSAMORO WOMEN COMMISSION OF THE BARMM, PROVIDING FOR ITS POWERS, FUNCTIONS AND COMPOSITION AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
signed_by: Atty. Ali Pangalian M. Balindong, Speaker
Prof. Raby B. Angkal, Secretary General
basic_information.effectivity: 15 days after publication in a newspaper of local circulation in the BARMM

citizen_summary.what_is_this_about: Creates the Bangsamoro Women Commission — the region's watchdog and policy body for women's rights, attached to the Office of the Chief Minister, with commissioners seated province by province.
citizen_summary.why_was_it_proposed: The Organic Law (RA 11054) requires the Bangsamoro Government to ensure women's representation and participation in governance. The act builds the machinery for that, and anchors itself on CEDAW and on UN Security Council Resolution 1325 on women in peacebuilding.
citizen_summary.what_will_change: There is now a standing body that can require every Bangsamoro ministry and office to submit its gender and development plan and budget, refer women needing help to the right agency, work with police and the Shari'ah and regular courts on gender-based violence, and accredit women's organisations.
who_will_be_affected: Women across the BARMM — the Commission is the region's primary policy-making, coordinating and monitoring body on women, gender and development
Every Bangsamoro ministry, agency and office, which can be required to submit GAD plans, budgets and implementation reports
Local government units in the region, whose gender development plans follow the Commission's guidelines
Non-Moro Indigenous Peoples and settler communities, represented by two ex-officio Commissioners who hold the right to vote
Women's and people's organisations, which the Commission may accredit
citizen_summary.when_will_it_take_effect: In force since 2020 — 15 days after publication in a newspaper of local circulation in the BARMM.

what_this_means_for_you.in_short: NOW LAW. If you are a woman in the BARMM, there is a Commission whose job is your rights — with a commissioner seated in your province, power to make ministries account for their gender plans, and a duty to refer your case to the agency that can act on it.
in_practice: A Commissioner with an office in each of Basilan, Sulu, Tawi-Tawi, Lanao del Sur, and Maguindanao
The Commission can require any ministry or office to submit its gender and development plan, budget and progress reports
It refers specific cases of women needing assistance to the agency that can help
It works with law enforcement and with the Shari'ah and regular courts on gender-based violence
It accredits women's and people's organisations working on women's rights
It convenes an advisory council that seats one woman each from youth, civil society, traditional leaders, Bangsamoro communities outside BARMM, and religious leaders

for_specific_groups.Women in the provinces: Section 13 requires each Commissioner to keep an office in the province she represents — the body is not only in Cotabato City.
for_specific_groups.Survivors of gender-based violence: The Commission is mandated to work with law enforcement and with both the Shari'ah and the regular courts, and to refer cases on.
for_specific_groups.Non-Moro Indigenous and settler women: Two ex-officio seats represent these communities, held by the heads of the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs and the office for settler communities — and those seats vote.
for_specific_groups.Women's organisations: You can seek accreditation, and a seat on the advisory council through the civil society slot.
for_specific_groups.Women seeking appointment: Qualifications: Filipino citizen, at least 25, 5 years' residence in the BARMM, a registered voter there, a record of leadership in government or women's organisations, and no conviction for a crime of moral turpitude.

what_this_means_for_you.where_this_applies: The whole BARMM, including Cotabato City and the 63 barangays of North Cotabato.
what_you_can_do: Approach the Commissioner for your province — each has an office there
Ask your LGU or a ministry for its gender and development plan; the Commission can require them to produce one
Bring a case needing assistance to the Commission for referral
Seek accreditation if you run a women's or people's organisation
watch_out_for: The Commission is a policy, monitoring and referral body — it does not itself prosecute, adjudicate or pay benefits.
It is attached to the Office of the Chief Minister, which supervises it, and the Chief Minister appoints all five voting commissioners.
Its initial appropriation was ₱30 million in total, which is small for a region-wide mandate.
A live bill, Parliament Bill 474, would convert the two ex-officio seats into regular Commissioner positions — see it for the current argument about this Commission's composition.

key_terms_explained.GAD plan: Gender and Development plan — the plan and budget each government office must produce for how its work serves women.
key_terms_explained.CEDAW: The UN Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women.
key_terms_explained.UNSCR 1325: The UN Security Council resolution on women, peace and security.
key_terms_explained.Ex-officio: Holding a seat by virtue of another office, rather than by separate appointment.
key_terms_explained.En banc: The whole Commission sitting together — its orders need the concurrence and signature of a majority of members.

benefits.headline: A standing body for women's rights, seated in every province, that can hold ministries to account.

direct_benefits.benefit: A Commissioner with an office in your province
direct_benefits.who_gets_it: Women in Basilan, Sulu, Tawi-Tawi, Lanao del Sur and Maguindanao

direct_benefits.benefit: Referral of a case needing assistance to the agency that can act
Accreditation for women's and people's organisations
direct_benefits.who_gets_it: Organisations working on women's rights in the Bangsamoro

direct_benefits.benefit: A seat on the advisory council
direct_benefits.who_gets_it: One woman each from youth, CSOs, traditional leaders, Bangsamoro communities outside BARMM, and religious leaders

indirect_benefits: Sex-disaggregated data generated with the planning authority, which is what evidence-based policy for women needs
Ministries and LGUs held to published gender plans and budgets
limitations: No cash benefit or entitlement for individuals.
No power to prosecute or adjudicate — it refers, monitors and recommends.
₱30 million initial funding against a region-wide mandate.

what_this_means_for_you.status_note: Passed 31 January 2020, approved by the Chief Minister on 13 February 2020.

for_citizens: None. The act imposes no duty, fee or filing on the public.
for_government: Ministries, agencies and offices may be required to submit GAD plans, budgets and implementation reports
LGUs follow the Commission's guidelines for their gender development plans

what_is_prohibited: The act defines no prohibited acts for the public and creates no offences.

penalties.for_citizens: None. The act creates no offence, fine or imprisonment.
penalties.for_officials: The Commission may suspend, dismiss or discipline its own officials and employees below Salary Grade 25.
penalties.note: The act provides no sanction against a ministry that fails to submit its GAD plan — compliance rests on monitoring and reporting, not penalty.

where_to_complain.first_stop: The Bangsamoro Women Commission, or the Commissioner for your province
where_to_complain.oversight: Office of the Chief Minister, which supervises the Commission
where_to_complain.note: The act creates no formal complaints or appeals procedure of its own.

everyday_scenarios: Sittie in Tawi-Tawi wants to know what her provincial government is doing for women. Her province has a seated Commissioner with an office there, and the Commission can require the LGU's gender development plan.
A women's cooperative in Lanao del Sur wants recognition to work with government on women's rights. Section 8(f) lets the Commission accredit it.

A survivor of gender-based violence needs somewhere to start. The Commission's mandate is to work with law enforcement and with the Shari'ah and regular courts, and to refer her case to the agency that can act — though the Commission itself does not prosecute.

key_provisions: Section 1 — Short title: the “Bangsamoro Women Commission Act of 2020”.

Section 2 — Policy: reaffirms women's role under the Organic Law (RA 11054), their rights to representation, lawful employment and protection from exploitation, abuse and discrimination under CEDAW, and their place at the forefront of peacebuilding under UN Security Council Resolution 1325.

Section 3 — Creates the Bangsamoro Women Commission, supervised by the Chief Minister, with the status of a Bangsamoro Government agency attached to the Office of the Chief Minister. It exercises corporate powers, has a seal, and may sue and be sued.

Section 4 — Mandate: promote, protect and uphold women's rights as human rights; work for the elimination of all discrimination against women; and act as the region's primary policy-making, coordinating and monitoring body on women, gender and development.

Section 5 — Composition: a Chairperson and four regular Commissioners representing Basilan (with Lamitan City), Sulu, Tawi-Tawi, Lanao del Sur (with Marawi City), and Maguindanao (with Cotabato City and the 63 barangays of North Cotabato); plus two ex-officio Commissioners for non-Moro Indigenous Peoples and settler communities, being the heads of the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs and the office for settler communities. The ex-officio Commissioners have the right to vote.

Section 6 — Qualifications: Filipino citizen, at least 25 years old, a resident of the BARMM for 5 years before appointment, a registered voter there, with a record of leadership in government or in women's organisations, and no conviction for a crime involving moral turpitude. A majority must hold a bachelor's degree or its equivalent.

Section 7 — The Chief Minister appoints the Chairperson and the 4 Commissioners. First terms are staggered — 5 years for the chairperson, four for 2 members, three for 2 members — then 3 years each. No member may serve more than two consecutive terms.

Section 8 — Powers: hire and promote personnel below Salary Grade 25; discipline staff below that grade; contract; acquire and dispose of property; solicit and accept grants, aid and donations from any legitimate entity, local or foreign; and accredit women's and people's organisations.

Section 9 — Functions: issue guidelines for the gender development plans of the Bangsamoro Government and LGUs; prepare the Bangsamoro Gender and Development plan; research; pilot programmes; recommend legislation to Parliament; require ministries to submit GAD plans, budgets and implementation reports; monitor compliance with CEDAW and UNSCR 1325 and take part in international reporting; generate sex-disaggregated data with the planning authority; refer women needing assistance to the right agency; work with law enforcement and the Shari'ah and regular courts on gender-based violence; and convene an advisory council seating one woman each from youth, civil society, traditional leaders, Bangsamoro communities outside the BARMM, and religious leaders.
Section 10 — A collegial body of seven. Orders and resolutions are rendered en banc and must bear the concurrence and signature of a majority of members; a majority is a quorum.

Section 11 — Structure: Offices of the Chairperson and Commissioners, an Executive Director heading the Secretariat, an Administrative and Finance Services Division, and a Technical Services Division of three units — Policy and Program Development, Monitoring and Evaluation, and Coordinating and Public Engagement.

Sections 12–14 — The Chairperson is paid at Salary Grade 28 and regular Commissioners at 27; each Commissioner keeps an office in the province she represents; and the Commission's budget is transferred directly to it.

Section 15 — Appropriations: ₱15,000,000 for Personal Services, ₱14,000,000 for Maintenance and Other Operating Expenses, and ₱1,000,000 for Capital Outlay, sourced from the Miscellaneous Personnel Benefits Fund and the Contingent Fund under Bangsamoro Act No. 3, with later requirements carried in the Bangsamoro Appropriations Act.
Section 18 — Takes effect 15 days after publication in a newspaper of local circulation in the BARMM.

related_legislation.related_note: Parliament Bill 474 (at First Reading) proposes converting this Commission's two ex-officio seats — the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs and the Office for Settler Communities — into regular Commissioner positions, by amending the Bangsamoro Administrative Code.

citizen_questions.q: What does the Commission actually do for me?
citizen_questions.a: It sets the region's policy on women, requires ministries and LGUs to produce gender plans and budgets, refers women needing assistance to the agency that can act, works with police and the Shari'ah and regular courts on gender-based violence, and accredits women's organisations. It does not prosecute or pay benefits.

citizen_questions.q: Is there someone from my province?
citizen_questions.a: Yes. Four regular Commissioners represent Basilan, Sulu, Tawi-Tawi, Lanao del Sur, and Maguindanao — and Section 13 requires each to keep an office in the province she represents.

citizen_questions.q: Who represents non-Moro Indigenous Peoples and settlers?
citizen_questions.a: Two ex-officio Commissioners: the heads of the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs and of the office for settler communities. They have the right to vote. A pending bill would turn these into regular Commissioner posts.

If you are a Filipino citizen, at least 25, have lived in the BARMM for 5 years, are a registered voter there, have held positions of responsibility and leadership in government or in women's or women-serving organisations, and have no conviction for a crime involving moral turpitude. The Chief Minister appoints.

citizen_questions.q: How much does it cost, and who pays?
citizen_questions.a: ₱30 million to start — ₱15M for salaries, ₱14M for operating expenses, ₱1M for capital outlay — drawn from the Miscellaneous Personnel Benefits Fund and the Contingent Fund, with later funding through the Bangsamoro Appropriations Act.
